Where it began

Chris Woakes was born in Birmingham on 2 March 1989 and went to school at Barr Beacon Language College in Walsall. He took up cricket at seven, first at Aston Manor and then at Walmley, but for a while football ran it close: he was a trainee winger at Walsall until he was 14.

He came through Warwickshire's age-group sides, the academy and the second team, played a few games for Herefordshire in 2006, and by 2008 was a regular in the Warwickshire first team, taking 42 Championship wickets and topping the county's averages.

The player

His England career began in Twenty20 cricket in Adelaide in January 2011, where he opened the bowling and then hit the winning runs. His Test debut came in the last match of the 2013 Ashes. He went on to play 62 Tests up to 2025, taking 192 wickets at 29.61 with five five-wicket hauls and a best of 6 for 17, and scoring 2,034 runs at 25.11.

Lord's brought out the best in him. In 2016 he took 11 for 102 there against Pakistan, and in August 2018 he made his only Test hundred on the same ground, 137 not out against India, which put his name on both honours boards.

What made him special

He was the kind of cricketer captains love, useful in every part of the game. In the 2019 World Cup he was player of the match in the semi-final against Australia and took three more wickets in the final, and he played every game of England's winning run at the 2022 T20 World Cup. Only six players were in both winning squads.

He often saved his best for when it was needed. Recalled for the third Test of the 2023 Ashes at Headingley, he took three wickets in each innings and then hit the winning runs, and his 19 wickets in the series made him England's player of the series. His first Test innings with the ball had brought one wicket for 96, so it is fair to say things improved.

Away from the middle

Woakes played his county cricket for Warwickshire, where as a young number nine he once made 131 not out and shared a stand of 222 with Jonathan Trott. He played in the IPL for Kolkata Knight Riders, Royal Challengers Bangalore and Delhi Capitals, and for Birmingham Phoenix in The Hundred. He was named a Wisden Cricketer of the Year, and he retired from international cricket in September 2025.

And finally

He is a devoted Aston Villa supporter, and for a while he might have chased a ball for a living instead of hurling one. Football's loss was very much English cricket's gain.
